spark.summary: Database isolation levels control what concurrent transaction anomalies—dirty reads, non-repeatable reads, phantom reads, and write skew—are permitted in exchange for lower locking or coordination overhead.
spark.keyTakeaway: Read Committed does not prevent lost updates or read skew; Snapshot Isolation prevents read anomalies via MVCC but still allows write skew unless you use explicit `SELECT FOR UPDATE` or true Serializable isolation.

concept.whyItMatters: Most databases default to Read Committed (PostgreSQL, Oracle) or Repeatable Read (MySQL InnoDB), which silently permit race conditions like double-spending, inventory overselling, and broken invariants under concurrent requests—bugs that pass all single-threaded unit tests.
whenToUse: Use Read Committed for high-throughput, independent single-row writes and non-critical reads where slight point-in-time skew is acceptable.
Use Snapshot Isolation / Repeatable Read for consistent multi-table reporting, backups, and read-only analytics without blocking writers.
Use Serializable (SSI or 2PL) or explicit `SELECT ... FOR UPDATE` when enforcing cross-row invariants (account balances, double-booking prevention, quota limits).
whenNotToUse: Blindly setting global `SERIALIZABLE` on high-contention OLTP workloads without retry logic, which causes high `40001` serialization-failure abort rates.
Using `READ UNCOMMITTED` for any financial, inventory, or user-facing state—dirty reads expose rolled-back data.
Relying on Repeatable Read alone (without row locks) for read-modify-write counters, which suffers from lost updates or write skew.
keyPoints: ANSI SQL anomalies: Dirty Reads (reading uncommitted writes), Non-Repeatable Reads (row changes between reads), and Phantom Reads (new rows match a `WHERE` predicate).

Beyond ANSI: Read Skew (seeing half of a transfer), Lost Updates (two concurrent `x = x + 1` reads), and Write Skew (two transactions read overlapping data and write disjoint rows, breaking an invariant).
MVCC (Multi-Version Concurrency Control): readers read a consistent snapshot (`xmin/xmax` or HLC timestamp) without blocking writers, and writers don't block readers.
Snapshot Isolation vs. Serializable: Snapshot Isolation eliminates read skew and phantoms, but only Serializable (e.g., Postgres SSI or Spanner 2PL+TrueTime) prevents Write Skew.
Application retry loops are mandatory: optimistic/SSI engines abort conflicting transactions with SQLSTATE `40001` (`serialization_failure`), requiring idempotent client retries.

examples.title: On-Call Doctor Write Skew under Snapshot Isolation
examples.scenario: A hospital scheduling app required at least 1 doctor on call per shift. Under PostgreSQL `REPEATABLE READ` (Snapshot Isolation), Alice and Bob both queried `SELECT COUNT(*) WHERE on_call = true` (saw `2`), and each updated their own row to `on_call = false`.
examples.outcome: Because they modified disjoint rows, Snapshot Isolation committed both—leaving 0 doctors on call. Switching the transaction to `SERIALIZABLE` (SSI) detected the rw-antidependency cycle and aborted Bob's commit with `40001`.

examples.title: Flash-Sale Inventory Lost Update under Read Committed
examples.scenario: Two checkout requests read `stock = 1` simultaneously under `READ COMMITTED`, computed `new_stock = 0` in application code, and ran `UPDATE inventory SET stock = 0 WHERE sku = 'X'`—overselling the last item.
examples.outcome: Replacing read-modify-write with an atomic `UPDATE inventory SET stock = stock - 1 WHERE sku = 'X' AND stock > 0 RETURNING stock` eliminated the race without escalating isolation.

tradeOffs.factor: Consistency Guarantees vs. Throughput / Abort Rate
tradeOffs.pro: Serializable isolation eliminates all concurrency anomalies, letting engineers reason about transactions as if they ran one-by-one.
tradeOffs.con: High-contention keys trigger frequent `40001` serialization aborts (under SSI) or lock waits (under 2PL), reducing effective throughput.

tradeOffs.pro: Pessimistic `SELECT FOR UPDATE` guarantees the winner finishes without wasted work when contention is high (> 10% conflict rate).
tradeOffs.con: Pessimistic locks hold resources across network round-trips and risk deadlocks; SSI excels when conflicts are rare.

tradeOffs.factor: MVCC Version Retention vs. Garbage Collection
tradeOffs.pro: Readers never block writers on long-running analytical queries.
tradeOffs.con: Long-running `REPEATABLE READ` transactions prevent `VACUUM` / undo-log purge, causing table bloat and OOM.

failureModes.name: Missing Retry Handler for SQLSTATE 40001
failureModes.description: Enabling `SERIALIZABLE` or `REPEATABLE READ` without exponential-backoff retries surfaces raw `could not serialize access` 500 errors to users.
failureModes.mitigation: Wrap serializable transactions in an idempotent retry loop (3–5 attempts with jittered backoff) at the repository/DAO layer.

failureModes.name: Write Skew on Disjoint Rows
failureModes.description: Assuming `REPEATABLE READ` (Snapshot Isolation) prevents all race conditions leads to broken cross-row invariants (e.g., double-booking a meeting room).
failureModes.mitigation: Use `SERIALIZABLE` isolation, materialize a parent lock row (`SELECT ... FOR UPDATE` on `rooms`), or use Postgres `EXCLUDE USING gist` constraints.

failureModes.name: Long-Lived Snapshot Bloat
failureModes.description: An idle-in-transaction `REPEATABLE READ` session stays open for 6 hours, blocking MVCC garbage collection across the entire database.
failureModes.mitigation: Set `idle_in_transaction_session_timeout = '30s'` and route long analytical exports to a read replica.

failureModes.name: Deadlock Cascades under 2PL
failureModes.description: Transactions acquire row locks in inconsistent order (`A -> B` and `B -> A`), stalling threads until the deadlock detector aborts one.
failureModes.mitigation: Enforce a canonical lock acquisition order (e.g., sort `account_id` ascending before `SELECT FOR UPDATE`).

commonMistakes: Believing PostgreSQL's `REPEATABLE READ` allows phantom reads—in Postgres it implements Snapshot Isolation, which actually prevents phantoms, unlike the ANSI minimum.
Confusing MySQL InnoDB's `REPEATABLE READ` (which uses gap locks on `FOR UPDATE` to prevent phantoms, yet still permits write skew on plain `SELECT`s) with `SERIALIZABLE`.
Doing `SELECT balance` -> check in Java/Python -> `UPDATE balance` under `READ COMMITTED` instead of atomic SQL updates or `FOR UPDATE`.
Holding a database transaction open while making an external HTTP/Stripe API call, exhausting connection pools and holding row locks.
Testing concurrency bugs with sequential integration tests instead of parallel stress tests (e.g., Jepsen/Elle or concurrent goroutines).

sections.content:
## The idea

Database isolation (the **I** in ACID) defines how much concurrency side effects one transaction is allowed to observe from others. The 1992 ANSI SQL standard defined four levels—**Read Uncommitted**, **Read Committed**, **Repeatable Read**, and **Serializable**—based on three phenomena (Dirty Read, Non-Repeatable Read, Phantom Read).

However, modern MVCC databases (PostgreSQL, MySQL InnoDB, CockroachDB) exposed critical gaps in the ANSI definitions: **Snapshot Isolation (SI)** prevents all three ANSI anomalies yet still suffers from **Write Skew** (where two concurrent transactions read an overlapping premise and write to disjoint rows, violating a global invariant). Achieving true **Serializability** requires either **Two-Phase Locking (2PL)** or **Serializable Snapshot Isolation (SSI)**.

## Concrete walkthrough

Trace **Write Skew** vs. **SSI Detection** on a `rooms(room_id, slot, booking_id)` constraint:

1. **Setup**: Room `101` at `10:00` has 0 bookings. Policy: at most 1 booking per `(room_id, slot)`.
2. **Snapshot Taken**: Tx1 and Tx2 both start under Snapshot Isolation at `T=100`.
3. **Concurrent Reads**: Tx1 queries `SELECT COUNT(*) FROM bookings WHERE room_id=101 AND slot='10:00'` (sees `0`). Tx2 runs the same query (also sees `0`).
4. **Disjoint Writes**: Tx1 inserts `(id=501, room=101, slot='10:00')`. Tx2 inserts `(id=502, room=101, slot='10:00')`. Because `501 != 502`, there is no row-level write-write conflict.
5. **Outcome**:
   - Under **Snapshot Isolation (`REPEATABLE READ` in Postgres)**: Both commit -> **double-booked**!
   - Under **Serializable (`SERIALIZABLE` SSI)**: Postgres tracks `SIREAD` predicate locks on the index range `(101, '10:00')`, detects the dangerous `rw-antidependency` cycle (`Tx1 reads -> Tx2 writes` and `Tx2 reads -> Tx1 writes`), commits Tx1, and aborts Tx2 with `SQLSTATE 40001`.

sections.content:
## How databases implement isolation levels

Two engines claiming the same ANSI level can behave differently:

- **PostgreSQL**: Uses pure MVCC. `READ COMMITTED` takes a fresh snapshot per statement; `REPEATABLE READ` implements **Snapshot Isolation** (one snapshot per transaction, prevents phantoms, allows write skew); `SERIALIZABLE` adds **SSI** (`SIREAD` locks).
- **MySQL InnoDB**: Uses MVCC for plain `SELECT`s and **Next-Key Locks** (record + gap locks) for `SELECT ... FOR UPDATE` / `UPDATE`. Plain `REPEATABLE READ` can still exhibit subtle write skew, whereas `SERIALIZABLE` converts every plain `SELECT` into `SELECT ... LOCK IN SHARE MODE` (2PL).
- **Distributed SQL (CockroachDB, Spanner)**: CockroachDB defaults directly to `SERIALIZABLE` using Hybrid Logical Clocks (HLC), write intents, and timestamp-pushing; Spanner uses 2PL + TrueTime atomic clocks for External Consistency.

## Isolation levels vs. anomalies matrix

| Isolation Level | Dirty Read | Non-Repeatable Read | Phantom Read | Read Skew | Lost Update | Write Skew |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Read Uncommitted** | Possible | Possible | Possible | Possible | Possible | Possible |
| **Read Committed** (PG Default) | Prevented | Possible | Possible | Possible | Possible | Possible |
| **Repeatable Read** (InnoDB Default) | Prevented | Prevented | Prevented (gap locks on writes) | Prevented | Possible (on plain read-then-write) | Possible |
| **Snapshot Isolation** (PG Repeatable Read) | Prevented | Prevented | Prevented | Prevented | Prevented (First-Committer-Wins) | Possible |
| **Serializable** (PG SSI / CockroachDB) | Prevented | Prevented | Prevented | Prevented | Prevented | Prevented |

## Failure modes

- **Silent Read Skew in Billing**: Generating a multi-table invoice under `READ COMMITTED` reads `orders` before a concurrent `INSERT` commits and `order_items` after, producing mismatched totals.
- **False-Positive SSI Aborts**: Because `SIREAD` locks operate at page or index-granularity under memory pressure, unrelated transactions on the same index page can trigger unnecessary `40001` aborts.
- **Gap-Lock Deadlocks in MySQL**: Concurrent `INSERT ... ON DUPLICATE KEY UPDATE` under InnoDB `REPEATABLE READ` acquires overlapping gap locks, causing frequent deadlock rollbacks (`Error 1213`).
- **Transaction Wraparound / Undo Bloat**: Long-running `REPEATABLE READ` transactions pin old MVCC tuple versions, degrading sequential scan performance.

sections.eyebrow: 06 / Choosing the right tool for the invariant
sections.content:
## Choosing the right tool for the invariant

You don't always need global `SERIALIZABLE` isolation to enforce correctness:

1. **Atomic Single-Statement Updates**: `UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance - 50 WHERE id = 1 AND balance >= 50` is safe even under `READ COMMITTED`.
2. **Database Constraints**: `UNIQUE` indexes and PostgreSQL `EXCLUDE USING gist` (e.g., non-overlapping booking ranges) enforce invariants at the engine level without application retry loops.
3. **Pessimistic Row/Parent Locking**: Lock a single parent entity (`SELECT * FROM rooms WHERE id = 101 FOR UPDATE`) to serialize concurrent child inserts.
4. **SSI (`SERIALIZABLE`) + Retries**: Best for complex multi-table invariants where locks would be too coarse or deadlock-prone.

## Practical checklist

- [ ] Never perform `SELECT` -> compute in app -> `UPDATE` under `READ COMMITTED`; use atomic SQL expressions or `SELECT ... FOR UPDATE`.
- [ ] Verify your specific engine's guarantees (e.g., Postgres `REPEATABLE READ` = Snapshot Isolation; CockroachDB = `SERIALIZABLE` by default).
- [ ] Implement an idempotent retry wrapper for `SQLSTATE 40001` (serialization failure) and `40P01` (deadlock).
- [ ] Keep transactions short: never hold a DB transaction open across external HTTP/RPC calls.
- [ ] Set `idle_in_transaction_session_timeout` to protect MVCC garbage collection from abandoned snapshots.

simulation.title: Interactive Simulation: Database Isolation Levels Anomalies

steps.title: 1. Normal Request Ingress
steps.explanation: Database isolation levels control what concurrent transaction anomalies—dirty reads, non-repeatable reads, phantom reads, and write skew—are permitted in exchange for lower locking or coordination overhead.

steps.title: 2. Core Execution & State Lookup
steps.explanation: MVCC Snapshot Engine applies the primary invariant and coordinates with SSI Conflict Detector.

steps.title: 3. Scale Spike / Failure Injection
steps.explanation: Under a 10x burst, SSI Conflict Detector experiences contention and tail-latency amplification.

steps.title: 4. Mitigation & Steady Recovery
steps.explanation: Wrap serializable transactions in an idempotent retry loop (3–5 attempts with jittered backoff) at the repository/DAO layer.

tipsAndTricks: Core mental model: Read Committed does not prevent lost updates or read skew; Snapshot Isolation prevents read anomalies via MVCC but still allows write skew unless you use explicit `SELECT FOR UPDATE` or true Serializable isolation.
Avoid trap: Believing PostgreSQL's `REPEATABLE READ` allows phantom reads—in Postgres it implements Snapshot Isolation, which actually prevents phantoms, unlike the ANSI minimum.
Avoid trap: Confusing MySQL InnoDB's `REPEATABLE READ` (which uses gap locks on `FOR UPDATE` to prevent phantoms, yet still permits write skew on plain `SELECT`s) with `SERIALIZABLE`.
When to reach for it: Use Read Committed for high-throughput, independent single-row writes and non-critical reads where slight point-in-time skew is acceptable.
When to reach for it: Use Snapshot Isolation / Repeatable Read for consistent multi-table reporting, backups, and read-only analytics without blocking writers.
